Hi Alex — great to meet today. Thanks for walking us through the use case. Short recap + a few asks so we can align pricing + an SLO-driven plan for the POC: 

Summary from our side:
- Goal: integrate a coding assistant into PointWave IDE for code completion and short explanations (gen length ~150–500 tokens, avg ~280 tokens).
- Target latency SLO: you mentioned p95 around 200–300ms for interactive UX.
- Expected QPS: baseline 8–12 QPS, peak spikes to ~40 QPS during team hours.
- Monthly token bands (rough): pilot 5–15M, short-term (6mo) 20–60M, scale >100M if adoption climbs.
- Procurement notes: net30, SOC2 evidence required (we can share), and a one-page mutual action plan would help procurement.

Ask for you: can you confirm the budget band you have in mind for the next 12 months and any committed spend thresholds you prefer? Also confirm whether the SLO above is a hard requirement or a target we should optimize toward.

Next steps from our side: we can produce a 2-week POC MAP and two cost scenarios (low-latency config vs cost-optimized config) with explicit $/1M token estimates. We’ll include suggested batching/streaming settings that drive the trade-offs.

I’ve attached a draft MAP + our latest pricing sheet for reference.

Thanks,

- Token volumes: these ranges look right. For budgeting assume a conservative 6–25M tokens in year one; optimistic scenario up to ~85M if adoption is strong.

Alex / team — looping in our pricing lead. High-level guidance (numbers are illustrative until we lock commitment terms):

- Low-latency SLO (p95 <= 250ms): recommended approach is a Dedicated reservation with streaming-enabled endpoints and modest batching (batch windows <50ms). Estimated unit: ~$18–$24 / 1M tokens depending on commit length and burst policy.

- Cost-optimized (p95 target < 450ms): Hosted with aggressive batching + prefix caching; unit: ~$9–$13 / 1M tokens on metered usage, or lower with a 12-mo commit.

What drives the difference: dedicated GPU pools and lower queuing variance for the low-latency option; streaming reduces token-latency but reduces batching efficiency, so units go up. Caching and quantization can lower token run costs but only if workload has reuse patterns.

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Hi all — quick engineering note on latency vs cost levers so you can map numbers to technical choices: 

- Streaming vs full-buffer: streaming returns tokens as they are decoded; this reduces perceived latency for interactive UX but prevents large batch aggregation. Typical trade: streaming can reduce median/user-visible latency by ~30–60ms, but p95 depends on tail queuing.
- Batching policy: increasing per-request batch sizes improves GPU utilization and reduces $/token, but introduces batching delay. For your SLO (p95 <= 250ms) we recommend a max batch wait of 25–50ms and concurrency tuning at the autoscaler to avoid queue build-up during spikes.
- Prefix/KV caching: if you have repeated prompts or context (e.g., shared workspace snippets), prefix caching can cut token compute by 15–40% for some flows.
- Dedicated pool sizing: for the estimated peak (~40 QPS with ~280 tokens/res), a small dedicated pool with autoscale headroom will flatten p95 tails vs hosted shared pools. Exact sizing depends on model choice and quantization.

Example back-of-envelope unit math (illustrative):
- Cost-optimized hosted: $11 / 1M tokens -> 25M tokens = $275/mo (~$3.3k/year) — note this is compute-only example; network/observability add-ons extra.
- Low-latency dedicated: $20 / 1M tokens -> 25M tokens = $500/mo compute-equivalent (higher if reserved capacity pricing includes minimums).

I can run a short simulator for your token distribution (if you share a small sample of typical prompt/response lengths) and give concrete per-1M numbers for both SLOs.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Solutions Architect
Redwood Inference
